caption: County of Los Angeles v. Mendez
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Clearly controlling excessive-force and Section 1983 damages decision omitted from the case corpus. Rejects the Ninth Circuit provocation rule: a separate Fourth Amendment violation cannot transform an otherwise reasonable use of force into excessive force, while leaving ordinary proximate-cause damages for the separate violation available.

caption: Zorn v. Linton
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Most recent controlling qualified-immunity excessive-force summary reversal found in the lane. Holds that Second Circuit precedent did not clearly establish that a warned rear-wristlock used to move a noncompliant sit-in protester violated the Fourth Amendment; adverse authority for force/QI pages.

caption: Nieves v. Bartlett
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling retaliatory-arrest rule omitted from the case corpus. Probable cause generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, with a narrow objective-evidence exception for offenses where officers typically exercise discretion not to arrest.

caption: Gonzalez v. Trevino
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling follow-on to Nieves omitted from the case corpus. Rejects the Fifth Circuit's overly cramped comparator requirement and permits objective evidence other than virtually identical non-arrests to invoke the Nieves exception.

caption: Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling retaliatory-arrest municipal-liability decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds that probable cause does not categorically bar a retaliatory-arrest claim against a municipality when the arrest allegedly implements an official retaliatory policy.

caption: Reichle v. Howards
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling retaliatory-arrest/QI bridge case omitted from the case corpus. Grants qualified immunity because it was not clearly established that a probable-cause-supported arrest could violate the First Amendment; useful predecessor to Nieves and Gonzalez.

caption: Hartman v. Moore
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling retaliatory-prosecution causation decision omitted from the case corpus and repeatedly used by retaliatory-arrest cases. Requires plaintiffs alleging retaliatory prosecution to plead and prove absence of probable cause.

caption: Manuel v. City of Joliet
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution/unlawful-pretrial-detention decision omitted from the case corpus. Resolves a circuit split by holding that the Fourth Amendment governs unlawful pretrial detention even after legal process; the Seventh Circuit was the outlier against ten other circuits.

caption: Thompson v. Clark
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution decision omitted from the case corpus. Resolves favorable-termination split: Second, Third, and Tenth Circuits required affirmative indication of innocence; Eleventh Circuit required only termination without conviction; SCOTUS adopted the latter rule.

caption: Chiaverini v. City of Napoleon
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution decision omitted from the case corpus. Resolves charge-by-charge probable-cause split: Sixth Circuit applied an any-valid-charge bar; Second, Third, and Eleventh Circuits allowed claims based on unsupported charges despite other valid charges.

caption: Culley v. Marshall
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling civil-asset-forfeiture due-process decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds that due process requires a timely forfeiture hearing for seized personal property but not a separate preliminary retention hearing; confirms the $8,850/Von Neumann timeliness framework.

caption: Timbs v. Indiana
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling forfeiture/excessive-fines decision omitted from the case corpus. Incorporates the Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause against the States and confirms that punitive civil in rem forfeitures remain subject to Austin.

caption: Austin v. United States
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling civil-forfeiture excessive-fines foundation omitted from the case corpus. Holds that forfeitures under 21 U.S.C. 881(a)(4) and (a)(7) are monetary punishment subject to the Excessive Fines Clause.

caption: United States v. Bajakajian
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling excessive-fines proportionality decision omitted from the case corpus. Establishes that punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause when grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense.

caption: Bennis v. Michigan
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling civil-forfeiture innocent-owner decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds that forfeiture of an innocent co-owner's interest did not violate Due Process or the Takings Clause where state law supplied no innocent-owner defense.

caption: United States v. $8,850
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling civil-forfeiture delay/due-process decision omitted from the case corpus. Applies Barker-style factors to whether post-seizure delay before a forfeiture proceeding denies a meaningful hearing at a meaningful time; reaffirmed by Culley.

caption: United States v. Von Neumann
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling civil-forfeiture due-process decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds that a timely forfeiture proceeding, without an additional remission procedure, supplies the post-seizure hearing required by due process; reaffirmed by Culley.

caption: Ziglar v. Abbasi
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Bivens limitation decision omitted as a case page. Establishes the modern new-context/special-factors barrier and labels Bivens extension a disfavored judicial activity, directly relevant to federal-officer liability.

caption: Egbert v. Boule
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Bivens decision omitted as a case page. Refuses Bivens remedies for First Amendment retaliation and border/immigration-adjacent Fourth Amendment excessive-force claims, sharply narrowing federal-officer damages liability.

caption: Hernandez v. Mesa
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Bivens/use-of-force decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds that Bivens does not extend to claims arising from a cross-border shooting by a U.S. Border Patrol agent, marking adverse federal-officer force authority.

caption: Martin v. United States
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling FTCA federal-law-enforcement liability decision omitted from the case corpus. Wrong-house FBI raid case holding that the law-enforcement proviso overrides only the intentional-tort exception, not the discretionary-function exception, and that the Supremacy Clause is not an FTCA defense.

caption: Owen v. City of Independence
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling municipal-liability decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds municipalities have no qualified or good-faith immunity from Section 1983 liability for their own constitutional violations, filling a Monell/QI omission.

caption: Board of County Commissioners of Bryan County v. Brown
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Monell culpability/causation decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds that an isolated hiring decision did not show deliberate indifference or moving-force causation for a later excessive-force injury; tightens single-incident municipal liability beyond Canton/Connick.

caption: Will v. Michigan Department of State Police
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Section 1983 defendant-identity decision omitted from the case corpus. Holds States and state officials sued in official capacity for damages are not Section 1983 persons, a core liability boundary for the category.

caption: Hafer v. Melo
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Controlling Section 1983 capacity decision omitted from the case corpus. Clarifies that state officials sued in personal capacity are Section 1983 persons and may be personally liable for damages for actions taken under color of state law.

caption: Brownback v. King
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Mention-only. Real federal-law-enforcement liability authority on the FTCA judgment bar, cited in Martin, but less directly tied to the category's page gaps than Martin/Egbert/Abbasi/Hernandez.

caption: Albright v. Oliver
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Mention-only. Important precursor rejecting a substantive-due-process malicious-prosecution theory and later cited by Manuel/Thompson, but fragmented and now better handled as background to Manuel and Thompson.

caption: Wallace v. Kato
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Mention-only. Section 1983 Fourth Amendment false-arrest accrual case adjacent to malicious prosecution, but not a page candidate for this lane because the more direct malicious-prosecution omissions are Manuel, Thompson, and Chiaverini.

caption: Calero-Toledo v. Pearson Yacht Leasing Co.
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Mention-only. Civil-forfeiture innocent-owner precursor repeatedly discussed in Bennis, but Bennis is the cleaner controlling page candidate for the modern innocent-owner constitutional rule.

caption: Millbrook v. United States
court: Supreme Court of the United States
justification: Mention-only. FTCA law-enforcement-proviso authority cited by Martin; real but less central to the wrong-house-raid/federal-officer liability gap than Martin itself.
